# Quick Transition

```{r}
#Last week we covered atomic vectors, coercion, and factors -- remember how our "card" object got turned entirely into character due to coercion? We'll reuse it today, but this time we'll AVOID coercion: with lists and data frames.
```

# Matrices

```{r}
#matrix() reshapes a vector into 2 dimensions (rows x columns). 
##By default it fills column by column:

die <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)

m <- matrix(die, nrow = 2)
m
```

```{r}
#With byrow = TRUE, it fills row by row instead:

m <- matrix(die, nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
m
```

# Lists

```{r}
#Last week "card" was an atomic vector, and coercion turned even the 1 into the string "1":

card_vector <- c("ace", "hearts", 1)
typeof(card_vector[[3]])  ## "character" -- coercion happened
```

```{r}
#list() is different: elements can STAY different types, no coercion happens.

card <- list("ace", "hearts", 1)
card

card[[3]]

typeof(card[[3]])  ## "double" -- still a number!
```
```{r}
#A more realistic use case: bundling different pieces of info about ONE participant together.
#This only works cleanly with a list -- an atomic vector would coerce everything to character.

participant <- list(name = "Ayla", age = 23, passed_screening = TRUE)
participant

typeof(participant$age)               ## "double" -- still a number
typeof(participant$passed_screening)  ## "logical" -- still TRUE/FALSE

#Preview: when you run t.test() or lm() later this semester, the result you get back
#is ALSO a list -- it bundles numbers, labels, and text together the same way.
```



# Data Frames

```{r}
#A data frame bundles equal-length vectors together as columns, forming a table. 
##It's actually a special list with the class "data.frame".

df <- data.frame(
  participant = 1:4,
  condition = c("treatment", "control", "control", "treatment"),
  score = c(88, 76, 81, 92)
)

df

typeof(df)   ## "list"
class(df)    ## "data.frame"
```


```{r}
#Note: (this will differ from the textbook's output -- not an error!): the book was written for an older R version. Since R 4.0, data.frame() no longer automatically converts character columns to factors. 

##When you run str(), you'll see the "condition" column as chr, not Factor.

str(df)
```

```{r}
#If you want a column to be a factor on purpose, wrap it explicitly with factor():

df$condition <- factor(df$condition)
str(df)
```

# Loading & Saving Data

```{r}
#write.csv() lets you save a data frame as plain text (.csv). row.names = FALSE stops R from adding an extra row-number column.

write.csv(df, file = "week4_demo.csv", row.names = FALSE)

getwd()  #Shows you where the file was saved
```

```{r}
#Load it back in with read.csv():

df2 <- read.csv("week4_demo.csv")
head(df2)
str(df2)

#Watch out: saving and reloading can sometimes silently change a column's type (e.g., "score" may come back as "int" instead of "num" here) -- so it's good practice to always check with str() after loading data. In upcoming weeks, we'll load the real TGSS survey data the same way.
```

##Different Formats

```{r}
#You can also export a data frame to other common formats researchers use:

#SPSS (.sav) -- needs the haven package (install.packages("haven") once, if you haven't already)
library(haven)
write_sav(survey, "survey.sav")

#Excel (.xlsx) -- needs the writexl package (install.packages("writexl") once, if you haven't already)
library(writexl)
write_xlsx(survey, "survey.xlsx")

#Reading them back in works the same way, just with matching functions:
survey_from_spss <- read_sav("survey.sav")
survey_from_excel <- readxl::read_excel("survey.xlsx")  # needs the readxl package
```
